item.title: Methodist Church President calls for nightclubs to close at 11pm and proposes National Day of Prayer
item.description: All nightclubs in Fiji should close at 11pm to allow parents to spend more time with their families, according to Methodist Church President Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou, who is also calling for a National Day of Prayer for people of all faiths. Reverend Dr Turagavou raised these issues during consultations on the Constitution Amendment Bill, saying there needs to be greater control over nightclub
item.content:encoded:
All nightclubs in Fiji should close at 11pm to allow parents to spend more time with their families, according to Methodist Church President Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou, who is also calling for a National Day of Prayer for people of all faiths.

Reverend Dr Turagavou raised these issues during consultations on the Constitution Amendment Bill, saying there needs to be greater control over nightclub operating hours and more emphasis on family responsibilities.

He says nightclubs have previously remained open until 1am, raising concerns about parents going out at night and leaving their children at home until the following morning.

Turagavou says this is an issue the country needs to seriously consider , as both mothers and fathers should return home earlier and spend time with their families.

He is proposing that all nightclubs close at 11pm to allow parents to return home earlier and fulfil their responsibilities towards their children and families.

The Methodist Church President also believes Fiji should have a National Day of Prayer, when people of different faiths can pray for the country.

He says the proposal does not mean everyone must gather under one roof, as people can pray from their homes or wherever they are.

Turagavou says Christians, Muslims, Hindus and members of other religious groups should all be encouraged to take part in praying for the nation.

He believes that when people pray collectively, God will hear their prayers.

His proposals focus on the importance of faith, family responsibilities and encouraging parents to spend more time with their children.

item.title: Turaga remains tight-lipped on widely circulated video, says he will speak after process is completed
item.description: Former Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga says he will not comment on the widely circulated video until all processes are completed. Turaga made the comment when asked whether he had reported the video to the Online Safety Commission, given that it was being widely circulated by some members of the public.
item.content:encoded:
Former Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga says he will not comment on the widely circulated video until all processes are completed.

Turaga made the comment when asked whether he had reported the video to the Online Safety Commission, given that it was being widely circulated by some members of the public.

He was also asked whether his account had been hacked or whether the post was accidental.

Turaga declined to provide further details, saying he would not make any comment for now.

He says he will be able to comment once all the processes are completed.

Turaga has still not clarified whether the video issue has been reported to the Online Safety Commission.

item.title: Cultural barriers make cancer discussions difficult for Lau women - Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau President
item.description: Women from the Lau Islands are being encouraged to undergo regular health checks and seek early medical attention, as cultural barriers continue to make discussions about cancer difficult. Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau President Rigieta Halofaki says many women are reluctant to visit hospitals for check-ups, prompting the organisation to invite representatives from the Fiji Cancer Society and the Min
item.content:encoded:
Women from the Lau Islands are being encouraged to undergo regular health checks and seek early medical attention, as cultural barriers continue to make discussions about cancer difficult.

Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau President Rigieta Halofaki says many women are reluctant to visit hospitals for check-ups, prompting the organisation to invite representatives from the Fiji Cancer Society and the Ministry of Health to raise awareness about cancer affecting women.

Speaking during the the celebration of International Rural Women's Day, Pinktober and Senior Citizens and Expo at the Seafarers Club in Walu Bay, Suva, Halofaki says the awareness sessions aim to help women understand what steps to take if they develop cancer.

She says breast and cervical cancer are among the conditions affecting women in Lau, although the organisation does not have data on the number of women affected.

Halofaki says discussing these health issues can be difficult within Fijian traditions, but awareness programmes provide an opportunity to share information and encourage women to seek medical help.

She says the celebration today also recognises elderly women and senior citizens for their years of service and contribution to Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau.

Halofaki says the organisation is also working on its strategic development plan, which focuses on rural development, education and preserving traditional Lauan handicrafts.

She says the plan has been revised to combine eight previous thematic areas into five, with a focus on supporting women from the islands and those living in Suva.

Halofaki says preserving traditional handicrafts is important as more companies commercialise such products.

She adds that education remains a priority for the organisation, which wants younger generations to continue pursuing educational opportunities.

Halofaki adds that the Women's Fund Fiji has supported the organisation's work over the past three years, while other activities are funded through fundraising and contributions from women in the different tikinas .

item.title: Fiji must address inequality, drugs and HIV alongside immunity debate – Tui Nayau
item.description: Fiji cannot achieve lasting reconciliation by addressing immunity alone while economic inequality, drug-related problems and HIV continue to affect communities across the country. Tui Nayau Ratu Tevita Lutunauga Kapaiwai Uluilakeba Mara says reconciliation requires more than changes to the law, and must also address the social and economic challenges facing Fijians.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji cannot achieve lasting reconciliation by addressing immunity alone while economic inequality, drug-related problems and HIV continue to affect communities across the country.

Tui Nayau Ratu Tevita Lutunauga Kapaiwai Uluilakeba Mara says reconciliation requires more than changes to the law, and must also address the social and economic challenges facing Fijians.

Speaking on the public consultations on the Constitution Amendment Bill, Ratu Tevita says he respects the Supreme Court's opinion on immunity, but believes the country must also confront the deeper issues that have contributed to social tensions.

He says many iTaukei families are still struggling to benefit from Fiji's economy, 56 years after the country gained independence.

Ratu Tevita says these economic concerns were among the issues exploited during the political upheavals of 1987 and 2000.

He stresses that taking power by force can never be justified, but says the underlying problems that were exploited during those periods must also be addressed if Fiji is to achieve lasting reconciliation.

Ratu Tevita also raised concerns about the impact of drugs and HIV on young people and communities, saying the vanua, churches, families and Government must work together to address these challenges.

He says national unity also requires respect, understanding and responsible leadership.

The Tui Nayau condemned threatening social media comments directed at people who criticised chiefs, saying Fiji's traditional leaders do not need to be defended through threats or intimidation.

He says while people should respect Fiji's chiefs and traditional institutions, criticism and disrespect should be answered with dignity rather than threats.

Ratu Tevita also stressed that Indo-Fijians, descendants of the girmitiya and every community that calls Fiji home belong to the country.

He welcomed recent comments by RFMF Commander Major General Ro Jone Kalouniwai that the people's vote must be protected and respected.

Ratu Tevita says Fiji now needs leaders at every level to use words that bring people together, address the challenges facing communities and find a common path towards national unity.

item.title: Rokotunidau’s bail hearing adjourned to Nov 5th
item.description: Saimoni Rokotunidau, who is charged with the attempted murder of a female police officer in Laqere and the unlawful possession of methamphetamine, had his bail hearing vacated this morning. The court was informed by his new lawyer that they are awaiting the discharge summary from his previous lawyer, Jerry Dinati.
item.content:encoded:
Saimoni Rokotunidau, who is charged with the attempted murder of a female police officer in Laqere and the unlawful possession of methamphetamine, had his bail hearing vacated this morning.

The court was informed by his new lawyer that they are awaiting the discharge summary from his previous lawyer, Jerry Dinati.

State lawyer Hezekiah Nofaga told the court that the trial is expected to take about one and a half weeks.

The pre-trial conference has been adjourned to November 5, when the bail hearing will also take place.

Rokotunidau is charged with one count each of attempted murder, unlawful possession of illicit drugs, going equipped, serious assault, and refusing to have his fingerprints and photographs taken.
